corpus_definition: A sudden shaking of the ground that causes damage.

forms.definition: a sudden, strong shaking of the ground that can break buildings
forms.example: The 1966 earthquake in Tashkent destroyed many old houses.

syn.note: Short, informal word for the same thing, common in news headlines.
A small shaking of the ground, often weaker than a full one.
Related: a smaller shaking that comes after the big one.

forms.note: There is no verb from this word. To talk about the action, say 'the ground shook'.
There is no adjective from this word. Use the noun before another noun: 'earthquake damage', 'an earthquake zone'.

context.text: Last night a small earthquake woke us up in Namangan. The windows shook, but nobody was hurt. My grandmother still remembers the big earthquake of 1966.

reviewer_note: Compound noun (earth + quake) with no derived forms; only one form exists, so the context uses it alone.

corpus_definition: Have a meal at a restaurant instead of your house.
particle_note: Not separable and has no object: 'We eat out on Fridays.' Add a place with at or in: 'eat out at a cafe'.

relations.note: Same meaning but more formal, often used for a nice dinner.
Related: leave home to have fun, which may or may not include a meal.
To have a meal at home instead of going to a restaurant.

context.text: We usually eat out on Friday evenings. Last week we ate out at a new plov centre near the bazaar, and it was cheaper than cooking at home.

reviewer_note: Intransitive phrasal verb; eat in given as the natural opposite.

corpus_definition: To make changes to a text or video to improve it.

forms.definition: the work of correcting and improving a text, film or video
forms.example: Video editing takes much longer than filming.

syn.note: Changing a text to make it better; used mostly for writing, not video.
Related: only fixing mistakes, not other improvements.

forms.definition: one change or a round of changes made to improve something
forms.example: I made a few quick edits before I sent the essay.

syn.note: Related: easy, general word; any change, not always an improvement.

forms.definition: one version of a book or newspaper printed at one time
forms.example: The new edition of the dictionary has many more words.
forms.note: Belongs to edit = prepare a book or newspaper for printing, not making small changes to a text or video.

forms.definition: to change a text or video to make it better or correct
forms.example: She edited the wedding video and added music.

syn.note: Change a text to improve it; not used for video.
Related: easy word; only fixing mistakes.
Related: read a text only to find small mistakes like spelling.
Related: easy word; look for problems, but maybe not change anything.

forms.definition: connected with preparing books, newspapers or programmes for people to read or watch
forms.example: She got an editorial job at a publishing house in Tashkent.
forms.note: As a noun, an editorial is a newspaper article that gives the newspaper's own opinion.

forms.definition: in a way connected with preparing books or newspapers for readers
forms.example: The magazine is editorially independent from its owners.

people.definition: a person whose job is to check and improve texts or films
people.example: The editor asked me to make the article shorter.

context.text: My brother films short videos about Samarkand. He edits them at night, and the editing often takes longer than the filming. Before he posts a video, he always makes a few last edits.

reviewer_note: Noun slot: editing (the activity) as main, edit (noun) as extra; edition and the noun editorial marked other_meaning; editor in people.

gate_overrides.msg_contains: noun 'edit': not in the dictionary as a noun
gate_overrides.reason: edit is a noun in the Oxford and Cambridge learner dictionaries ('make a few edits'); WordNet 3.1 only has the verb.
edition is edit + the suffix -ion (a derivation), not a compound of two words; it is the 'book version' meaning, kept as other_meaning.

corpus_definition: A result or change caused by something.

forms.definition: a change or result that happens because of something
forms.example: The hot weather had a bad effect on the cotton harvest.
forms.note: Don't confuse with the verb affect: 'Rain affects the crops' but 'Rain has an effect on the crops'.

syn.note: Easy, very close word for what happens because of something.
A result, often a bad one; a little more formal.
A strong or important effect.
The final result of a plan, game or situation.
Related: the power to change something, often slowly.

ant.note: The cause makes something happen; the effect is what happens.

forms.definition: how well something works and gives the result you want
forms.example: Doctors are testing the effectiveness of the new medicine.

syn.note: Related: easy word for getting the result you wanted.
Related: working well without wasting time or money.

ant.note: Not working well or not giving the result you want.

forms.definition: to make a change or plan happen
forms.example: The new manager effected many changes in the company.
forms.note: Belongs to effect = make something happen (formal). Learners usually need the verb affect instead, which is a different word.

forms.definition: working well and giving the result that you want
forms.example: Drinking a lot of water is an effective way to feel better.

syn.note: Easy word: getting the result you wanted.
Related: easy word; helping you do something.
Related: working well without wasting time or money. Not the same word.

ant.note: Not working well or not giving the result you want.

forms.definition: in a way that works well and gives the result you want
forms.example: Our teacher explains grammar very effectively.
forms.note: It also means 'in fact' or 'almost': 'The game was effectively over.'

syn.note: Easy word: in a way that gets the result you wanted.
Related: easy, very general word.

ant.note: In a way that does not work or give the result you want.

context.text: The new medicine had a strong effect on my cough. It was so effective that I was back at school in two days. The doctor said it works most effectively if you take it after food.

reviewer_note: Effect/affect trap noted on the noun and the verb; verb effect (formal 'make happen') is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: A person who is paid to do a job for someone else.

forms.definition: a person who works for a company or another person for money
forms.example: The bank has more than two hundred employees in Tashkent.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word; often used for people who work with their hands.
One person who works in an office, shop, school or hotel.
Related: formal word for all the people who work in a company, not one person.

forms.note: The opposite partner word is employer (see People & things).

forms.definition: the state of having a paid job
forms.example: It is hard to find employment in small villages.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word.
Related: easy word; a job is one position, employment is the general state.
Related: formal word for the kind of job you do.

ant.note: The state of not having a paid job.

forms.definition: to give someone a job and pay them for it
forms.example: The new factory will employ about five hundred people.
forms.note: In formal English it can also mean 'to use': 'employ a new method'.

syn.note: Very close; hire is more common in American English and in speaking.
British English, a little informal: 'The shop is taking on new staff.'
Related: look for and choose new people to join a company.

ant.note: Formal: tell someone they no longer have their job.
Informal: make someone leave their job.

forms.definition: having a job that you are paid for
forms.example: My sister is employed as a nurse at the city hospital.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word: 'a working mother'.

ant.note: Without a paid job.

forms.definition: having the skills that companies want when they choose workers
forms.example: Learning English makes young people more employable.

ant.note: Not able to get a job, for example because of no skills.

people.definition: a person or company that pays people to work for them
people.example: My employer gives me two weeks of holiday every year.

context.text: Aziz is an employee at a bank in Tashkent. The bank employs over two hundred people, and many students hope to find employment there after university.

reviewer_note: Two rows, same meaning, merged (B1). Headword is a person noun, so it stays the main noun; employer goes in people and as the antonym.

corpus_definition: A person or company that gives people jobs to do for money.

forms.definition: a person or company that gives people jobs and pays them
forms.example: The biggest employer in our town is the textile factory.

syn.note: Related: easy, informal word for the person in charge of you; an employer can also be a company.
Related: easy word; many employers are companies.
Related: the person who controls your work, who is often an employee too.

forms.note: The opposite partner word is employee (see People & things).

forms.definition: the state of having a paid job
forms.example: The new airport will bring employment to the region.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word.
Related: easy word; a job is one position, employment is the general state.

ant.note: The state of not having a paid job.

forms.definition: to give someone a job and pay them for it
forms.example: The hotel employs ten cooks in the summer.
forms.note: In formal English it can also mean 'to use': 'employ a new method'.

syn.note: Very close; hire is more common in American English and in speaking.
British English, a little informal: 'The shop is taking on new staff.'

ant.note: Formal: tell someone they no longer have their job.
Informal: make someone leave their job.

forms.definition: having a job that you are paid for
forms.example: Only half of the people in the village are employed.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word: 'a working mother'.

ant.note: Without a paid job.

forms.definition: having the skills that companies want when they choose workers
forms.example: Good computer skills make you more employable.

people.definition: a person who is paid to work for a company or person
people.example: Every employee gets a free lunch at the factory.

context.text: My employer is a small IT company in Samarkand. It employs twenty young people, and everyone employed there gets free English lessons.

reviewer_note: Two rows, same meaning, merged (lowest CEFR B1). Headword is a person noun, so it stays the main noun; employee goes in people and as the antonym. Boss kept as related, not synonym, because an employer can be a company.

corpus_definition: To keep people interested and happy.

forms.definition: shows, films, music or games that people enjoy
forms.example: There was music and dancing for entertainment at the wedding.

syn.note: The feeling or activity of having fun; a little old-fashioned.
Related: easy word for enjoyment, not the shows themselves.
Related: things you do in free time to relax, like sport.

forms.definition: to keep people interested and happy, for example with a show
forms.example: A magician entertained the children at the birthday party.
forms.note: It can also mean to invite guests and give them food and drink: 'We often entertain on Sundays.'

syn.note: Very close; amuse often means making people laugh.
Related: make someone very pleased.
Related: easy word; make people want to know more, not always fun.

ant.note: Make people tired because something is not interesting.

forms.definition: fun and interesting to watch, read or listen to
forms.example: The comedy show was really entertaining.

syn.note: Very close; amusing often means funny.
Easy word: something you enjoy.
Related: easy word; it keeps your attention but may not be fun.

ant.note: Not interesting at all.
Not exciting or interesting.

forms.definition: feeling interested and happy because something is fun
forms.example: The cartoons kept the kids entertained for an hour.

syn.note: Close; amused often means you find something funny.

ant.note: Tired and unhappy because nothing is interesting.

forms.definition: in a fun and interesting way
forms.example: He writes entertainingly about his travels in Central Asia.

syn.note: Close; amusingly usually means in a funny way.

people.definition: a person whose job is to sing, dance or tell jokes for people
people.example: The entertainer sang songs and told jokes at the party.

context.text: At my cousin's wedding, a famous singer entertained the guests all evening. Everyone said the show was very entertaining, and the children stayed entertained until midnight.

reviewer_note: Anchored to 'keep people interested and happy'; the 'have guests' use is mentioned in the verb note only.

corpus_definition: Something that is interesting and gives you enjoyment.

forms.definition: shows, films, music or games that people enjoy
forms.example: Television is the main entertainment for many old people.

syn.note: The feeling or activity of having fun; a little old-fashioned.
Related: easy word for enjoyment, not the shows themselves.

forms.definition: to keep people interested and happy, for example with a show
forms.example: The street musicians entertained the tourists in Registan Square.

syn.note: Very close; amuse often means making people laugh.
Related: make someone very pleased.

ant.note: Make people tired because something is not interesting.

forms.definition: fun and interesting, so you enjoy it
forms.example: Our history teacher tells very entertaining stories.

syn.note: Very close; amusing often means funny.
Easy word: something you enjoy.
Easy, informal word: 'The game was fun.'
Related: easy word; it keeps your attention but may not be fun.

ant.note: Not interesting at all.
Not exciting or interesting.

forms.definition: feeling interested and happy because something is fun
forms.example: The puzzle kept me entertained on the long train ride.

syn.note: Close; amused often means you find something funny.

ant.note: Tired and unhappy because nothing is interesting.

forms.definition: in a fun and interesting way
forms.example: The guide talked entertainingly about the old city.

syn.note: Close; amusingly usually means in a funny way.

people.definition: a person whose job is to sing, dance or tell jokes for people
people.example: He works as an entertainer on cruise ships.

context.text: The new Uzbek comedy film is really entertaining. The actors entertain you from the first minute, so it is perfect entertainment for a family evening.

reviewer_note: Headword is the -ing adjective, so it is the base of the adjective slot; entertain is listed as the verb it comes from.

corpus_definition: Shows, films, or games that people enjoy.

forms.definition: shows, films, music or games that people watch or play for fun
forms.example: The hotel offers live music and other entertainment every night.

syn.note: The feeling or activity of having fun; a little old-fashioned.
Related: easy word for enjoyment, not the shows themselves.
Related: things you do in free time to relax, like sport.
Related: free time when you are not working.

forms.definition: to keep people interested and happy, for example with a show
forms.example: Clowns entertained the crowd before the concert started.

syn.note: Very close; amuse often means making people laugh.

ant.note: Make people tired because something is not interesting.

forms.definition: fun and interesting to watch, read or listen to
forms.example: The football match was more entertaining than I expected.

syn.note: Very close; amusing often means funny.
Easy word: something you enjoy.

ant.note: Not interesting at all.

forms.definition: feeling interested and happy because something is fun
forms.example: The games kept the guests entertained all afternoon.

ant.note: Tired and unhappy because nothing is interesting.

forms.definition: in a fun and interesting way
forms.example: The book is entertainingly written and easy to read.

syn.note: Close; amusingly usually means in a funny way.

people.definition: a person whose job is to sing, dance or tell jokes for people
people.example: The entertainer made everyone laugh at the New Year party.

context.text: Tashkent has a lot of entertainment for young people, from cinemas to concerts. Street musicians entertain people in the parks, and the shows are free and entertaining.

reviewer_note: Uncountable noun in this meaning; the 'industry' use (the entertainment business) is the same meaning and needs no separate map.

corpus_definition: Feeling very interested and excited about something.

forms.definition: a strong feeling of excitement and interest in something
forms.example: The children showed great enthusiasm for the football lessons.

syn.note: Easy word; excitement is often short, enthusiasm can last a long time.
Strong wish to do something soon.
A very strong love for something, like music or sport.
Related: easy word, but much weaker.

ant.note: Not caring or not being interested at all.
Formal: no interest and no energy to do anything.

forms.definition: to talk about something in a very excited way
forms.example: She enthused about her trip to Khiva for an hour.

syn.note: Related, informal: praise something very strongly.

forms.definition: feeling or showing a lot of excitement and interest
forms.example: The students were very enthusiastic about the school trip.

syn.note: Easy word; excited is often about something that will happen soon.
Wanting very much to do something.
British English: 'keen on football'.
Stronger: having very strong feelings about something.
Related: easy word, but much weaker.

ant.note: Not interested or excited.
Easy: not wanting to know or do more.

forms.definition: in a very excited and interested way
forms.example: The fans cheered enthusiastically when the team scored.

syn.note: With a strong wish to do something.
Easy word, in an excited way.
Related: with strong interest.

ant.note: Without wanting to do it.

people.definition: a person who is very interested in a hobby or activity
people.example: He is a car enthusiast and reads every car magazine.

context.text: Our new English teacher is very enthusiastic. Her enthusiasm is so strong that even the quiet students now answer questions enthusiastically.

reviewer_note: Two rows, same meaning, merged (lowest CEFR B1). Affix -ic only (enthusiast + -ic); no -ly split claimed because 'enthusiastical' is not a word.
